tables.how: Every line of the Controller's payment file, fiscal 2019 to fiscal 2027 to date (to 9 November 2026), added up by payee, department, contract, purchasing rule and year. Two years are shown: the year the voucher was issued, read from its running number (scripts/lib/vouchers.py), and the fiscal year the file lists the line under, which for some lines is later. Each distinct wording of the purchasing rule is sorted into a route by the rule of the analysis the case quotes: emergency; sole source (with the Health Department's own sole-source list); bidding waived by ordinance; other wordings that say not bid or no bid. Agreements with other public bodies, purchases through a hospital buying consortium and small purchases a department may make itself are left out. For fiscal 2019 to 2026 the rows add up to $4,076,568,537: emergency $1,489,258,187, sole source $1,522,466,122, ordinance waivers $761,843,561, other not-bid rules $303,000,667; that is 7.5% of the $54.52 billion of payments that record any rule. Rows for fiscal 2027 to date are listed too; with them, payments under emergency rules come to $1,506,812,039.
tables.limits: Each route is written into the Administrative Code with a stated condition: a real emergency, a real single source, a class of work the Board has excused from bidding. The rule is the one staff keyed on the payment, and an emergency wording can stay on a grant after a Board waiver has taken its place. $51,520,851 keyed under these rules was issued in fiscal 2018 or earlier and filed under a later year; it is in none of these rows. 56 rows are payments to payees whose name reads as a private person's; those names are withheld. A payment is money paid for work under a contract, not a loss. The payment file starts in July 2018; near the turn of a year the voucher number dates a payment to within a few days.

tables.how: Six tests, each from a different file, joined on the supplier’s name: (1) a contract since July 2018 awarded as sole source or under another "not bid" rule; (2) a contract under an ordinance that waives bidding, or on the lists of contracts excused from the local-business rule; (3) $100,000 or more paid under emergency powers, or an emergency contract; (4) a Board resolution approving its agreement after the term began (the “retroactive” results); (5) an agreement that at least doubled through amendments (the site’s “Audits and official documents” page, the 60 rows it lists and its organization signals); (6) a contract set between $9.5 million and $10 million, under the amount that needs a Board vote (the “contract thresholds” results). Ranked by number of kinds, then by City payments since fiscal 2019.
tables.limits: A large provider of homelessness or health services will meet several simply because of its size and its field: the Board waived bidding for that work, the pandemic put it under emergency rules, and the Board’s calendar makes late approvals common. The count is a way to choose which files to read first, not a score of conduct. Name match across six files; other public bodies are left out. The amendment test covers only the agreements listed in the site’s “Audits and official documents” page. The paid figures count payments issued in fiscal 2019 or later, which is read from the voucher number and not from the year the file lists a line under; $1.08 billion that the whole payment file lists under those years was issued earlier and is left out.
